# 时间·变化·过程 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 6 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景；目标词**加粗**，展开"本篇生词"可遮释义自测。



### The Clock's Long Shadow

Long before **DST** was invented to squeeze an extra hour of light from the reluctant sun, people read time in simpler contrasts: **dawn**, when the sky cracked pale and cold over the fields, and **dusk**, when the same fields dissolved into shadow. Between those two poles, the day ran its **cycle** — not always tidily, not always on schedule, but always forward.

Civilizations, too, moved in cycles. Each **epoch** announced its own **advent** with fanfare, then quietly began to **decay**. What an **eon** of geology accomplishes in stone, a century of politics manages in the reputations of empires. Power was in **flux**: it rose, peaked, and entered its **ebb** before anyone had quite noticed the turn. And what **ensued** was rarely the clean break the victors promised — more often a long **hiatus**, a gap in the record, a silence that only later generations could read as transition.

Progress was seldom free of **lag**. Ideas that would one day remake the world spent **prior** decades ignored, their champions dismissed as **tardy** arrivals to conversations that had not yet started. A thinker might endure a lonely **stint** at the margins before the age finally **morphed** around their insight. Change did not announce itself; it accumulated. One **nonce** observation became a pattern; a pattern **begot** a theory; the theory, once it **ceased** to be controversial, hardened into common sense and eventually into **relic**.

In the **midst** of it all, individuals felt only the grain of the immediate: the **haste** with which a deadline approached, the need to **hurry** a decision before circumstance decided for them, the way a good season could **elapse** before one had properly enjoyed it. Those who learned to **forego** urgency — to let time work on a problem — often found that what looked like the **demise** of a plan was merely its dormancy. The thing would **recur**, altered and stronger. It always did. Whatever came before had not been wasted; it had simply been **altering** itself, grain by grain, into whatever came next.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### The Clock That Cannot Be Rewound

At the **outset**, the old **sundial** stood in the garden like a patient teacher, its shadow **ticking** across stone as the morning light climbed. The village was **nascent** then — a **budding** cluster of rooftops and mud lanes where every **grownup** still remembered the smell of **infancy**, and the young had not yet learned that time moves in only one direction.

Those early decades felt **cyclical**, the seasons **preceding** each other with a kind of comfort. In the long **interim** between harvests, life seemed to enter a **dormant** **stasis** — fields resting, ambitions quietly **slumbering** in the cold. Yet beneath that stillness the world was already shifting. Fortunes began to **crumble** and **dwindle**; old certainties that once felt **mature** and solid turned brittle. Anxiety **loomed** on the horizon long before anyone named it, and the **lagging** signs of decay were easy to miss when you were busy tending to **recess** and routine.

The hardest lesson was that you cannot **rewind** the tape. What the **bygones** held — the laughter, the quarrels, the long afternoons when light would **linger** on the water — could only be **relived** in memory, never in fact. Grief, if left alone, tends to **regress** into numbness; but numbness, too, will eventually **subside** if you do not let sorrow **retard** the slow work of healing. Some mornings a person must simply **commence** again: let the old aches **perish**, refuse to let the fear of what is **looming** become an excuse for **stasis**. At **last**, the **kickoff** of a new chapter rarely announces itself with fanfare — it arrives quietly, the way dawn does, and you only recognize it looking back.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### The Long Arc of a River Valley

**Prior to** the age of maps, people read time through the land itself. In the **forenoon**, when mist still clung to the ridgeline, elders would point to the layered cliffs and speak of **antiquity** — of a world so old that the **Jurassic** strata beneath their feet had once been seabed. Nothing about that deep past felt **ephemeral**; it pressed against the present like stone.

Yet change is never still. Rivers **stagnate** only in drought; the rest of the year they cut and carve, and the valley records each **upheaval** in silt and scar. **Hitherto** the floodplain had held its shape, but the spring thaw brought a **reversal** — channels jumped their banks, old sandbars **perished**, and **emerging** islands rearranged the whole lower reach. Farmers watched the **climactic** surge and then the slow **cessation** of the waters, knowing the **aftermath** would demand new seed-lines, new fences. Progress is rarely steady; it comes **fitfully**, **alternate** seasons of loss and **flourish**.

By midsummer the valley had reached a kind of **maturity**. The river ran clear, grasses achieved an **enduring** green, and children played on banks that had looked **imminent**ly dangerous only weeks before. But the calendar pressed on regardless. A **countdown** had already begun in the thinning light — the **temporal** window before first frost was shorter than it felt. Elders sensed the **exigency** and moved to **expedite** the harvest, unwilling to let abundance **intermit** into waste. They scheduled no **downtime** until the grain was in.

What the valley taught was the **emergence** of pattern from apparent chaos: a **fleeting** flood becomes the foundation of next year's soil; a **cessation** of growth precedes the deepest root-work; even the **obituary** of a season is a prologue. Resting in that knowledge, the people accepted the rhythm — not as surrender to **eternity**, but as literacy in time itself.

### When the Sandglass Runs Low

**Antecedent** civilizations understood time not as a line but as a wheel. They watched the **solstices** mark the sky's turning points, and **forthwith** built stone calendars to honour each shift. The **sandglass** was their intimate companion — a quiet, **recurring** witness to how moments slipped away. In those **primaeval** ages, change moved on a vast **timescale**, and yet even the most **eventless** stretches of pastoral life were **indelibly** scored by the seasons. Nothing stayed **suspended** for long; even the stillest valley was **eternally** in motion beneath its surface.

Then came the centuries that **transformed** everything. The **preceding** order — slow, ceremonial, tied to the solstice fire — began to **phase out** as new rhythms took hold. Each **milestone** arrived as a **precursor** to the next upheaval, and historians would later remark, with the benefit of **hindsight**, that every decisive shift had its **opportune** moment, a brief and **transient** window in which the old could be **supersede**d before it calcified again. What **transpired** across each **trimester** of a century might only become legible in the **follow-up** generations who inherited the wreckage and the gifts alike.

The hardest lessons concern **prolonged** waiting. A **lingering** illness, a **sustained** grief, a **premortal** stillness — these stretch a person across time in ways that no calendar can measure. **Hereafter**, wrote one forgotten essayist, the **tardiness** of healing should not be mistaken for failure; slow change is still change. **Whereupon** he closed his journal, set down his pen, and let the **sandglass** run.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### When a Century Becomes a Breath

In **retrospect**, every great civilization appears to have followed the same arc. What begins as a **primordial** stirring — a handful of people trading ideas across a fire — grows into something vast and bewildering. A **burgeoning** settlement becomes a city; a city becomes an empire; and before the **centennial** torch is even lit, the founders are already **posthumous** figures, their names carved in stone rather than spoken aloud. Each **predecessor** believed their own age to be the **culmination** of all that came before, never suspecting they occupied merely the **penultimate** chapter of a far longer story.

Change never **take place** at a single moment — it unfolds across **successive** waves, each **intervening** generation inheriting a world slightly altered from the one before. Some shifts are **transitory**, lasting no longer than a **nanosecond** in historical time; others **perpetuate** themselves across a **millennial** span, reshaping the very vocabulary we use to think. What **chronically** ails a society — the slow **degenerate** erosion of trust, the **alternating** bursts of reform and reaction — rarely announces itself. It accumulates quietly, the way a river carves a canyon: invisible until the canyon is there.

A **provisional** truce is signed, and a **transition** begins. Planners draw up **preliminary** blueprints for a new order. A **centenarian** who lived through the **millennium**'s turn watches from her window as her grandchildren move at speeds she cannot follow, acting **prematurely** on hopes that have not yet ripened. The city throws a festival to **commemorate** its founding — **prime time** broadcast, lights everywhere — promising that the memory will be kept in **perpetuity**. But the **recurrence** of history is its own quiet irony: **millennial** promises, **prehistoric** fears, and the **succession** of dawns that neither confirms nor denies either.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### When Time Folds Back on Itself

The geologist spread her notes across the table, arranging them in **chronological** order — oldest strata at the left, youngest at the right. Her life's work was the **Mesozoic Era**, that vast corridor of deep time when dinosaurs ruled and the continents still drifted in slow, **successional** waves of collision and rifting. She had spent thirty years tracing the **vicissitudes** of climate locked inside limestone and shale, each layer a frozen moment in a process that **revolutionized** our understanding of how life adapts to change.

Her research, **coincidentally**, had been published the same week as a major **commemoration** at the university — a century since the founding of the geology department. At the ceremony, a colleague delivered a **retrospective** lecture on how plate tectonics had, **simultaneously**, unsettled and unified three separate fields of science. The **synchronization** of those intellectual revolutions, he argued, was no accident; paradigm shifts tend to cluster. The audience laughed when he admitted that he had nearly missed his own talk, having **procrastinated** all week on finishing his slides — **procrastination**, he quipped, being one human habit that no amount of geological time seems to cure.

Outside, rain fell in **intermittent** bursts, drumming the courtyard in fits and starts. A junior researcher lingered by the door, watching it. She was the department's youngest hire, beginning what might become a **cradle-to-grave** devotion to the same ancient rock record her mentor had given her life to. She had already learned to **put something off** when the evidence was incomplete rather than rush to conclusions. And she was learning, too, the quieter lesson the geologist's career embodied: that **in hindsight**, the slowest processes — erosion, drift, the patient turning of epochs — are always the ones that change everything.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
